baslik: Frontier AI cleared every OT attack goal Booz Allen set in its lab
govde:
Frontier AI cleared every OT attack goal Booz Allen set in its lab

Booz Allen set frontier AI models against an isolated industrial-control testbed in its Chantilly, Virginia lab and watched them clear all eight attack objectives it had defined.

The Booz Allen frontier AI OT test architecture (Source: Booz Allen)

The models mapped the network, tied equipment to known weaknesses, wrote working exploits, pivoted into the systems that run production, and in the last test found a robotic arm, took administrative control, and moved it.

The testbed stood in for a manufacturing plant. Hundreds of IT and operational technology devices, real controllers, a SCADA platform, a motor drive, sensors, and that arm, wired into the layered zones a working factory uses.

In one run a model went from breaching the perimeter to acting inside the control zone in just over 16 minutes, which leaves a defender working at human speed almost no room to step in. Under the test’s rules, the models paused for human sign-off before anything physical happened.

The operators handed the models subnet boundaries and nothing else: no code, no engineering documents, no OT guidance. From that alone, the models built detailed plans. In one test a model noticed a protective relay, the device that trips breakers when it senses an electrical fault, broadcasting the same unanswered network request once a second. It flagged the relay as safety-critical and worked out on its own how to impersonate the communications partner the relay kept calling for, a path that could let it listen in and, under the right conditions, take control.

The models also recovered from dead ends. In the SCADA test, SCADA being the software operators use to watch and command a plant, a model first edited the wrong version of the operator interface, saw nothing change on the displays, then listed live sessions, found editable code in the exported project, rebuilt its payload, and pushed a full-screen takeover to the control room

baslik: Most high-severity cloud security findings are downgraded once an AI agent checks the environment
govde:
Most high-severity cloud security findings are downgraded once an AI agent checks the environment

Cloud security platforms turn every failed rule into a finding, and those findings pile up in queues sorted by severity. Research from Sola Security tested what happens to that order when each finding gets checked against the environment where it lives.

The researchers, Leon Goldberg and Gal Engelberg, built an AI agent that re-grades findings raised by third-party cloud security platforms. They ran it on 9,967 HIGH findings from two commercial platforms in eight production environments, and the agent changed the grade of 75.1% of them. Most moved down (58.5%), and 16.6% moved up.

One severity for every environment

The severity on a cloud finding comes from the rule that raised it. Each of 599 vendor rules issued exactly one severity over 99,073 failing findings, regardless of the resource or environment involved. “A static severity reflects the risk of the condition in general,” the researchers wrote, and “a queue ordered by it is ordered by the general case.”

“A rule carries the context its author can encode once for every environment,” they noted. “The context that decides what the condition is worth in a given environment lies elsewhere.” That includes whether the flagged resource is attached to anything and whether a workload runs on it.

Scoring standards reserve a place for this context. CVSS includes environmental metrics that adjust a base score to a particular deployment, and NIST risk assessment guidance ties likelihood to the controls in place. “A static severity leaves that place empty,” the researchers observed.

The agent’s evidence rules

For each finding, the agent forms a theory of how an attacker would exploit the problem, then collects evidence from the resource’s configuration, the resources connected to it, and data held by other security products.

Under the agent’s evidence policy, “raising a severity needs more evidence than lowering it.” L

baslik: Microsoft’s new model helps AI agents judge their next move
govde:
Microsoft’s new model helps AI agents judge their next move

Microsoft-Decision-1 is a small decision-scoring model. Given a situation, a question and a fixed set of answer options, it returns a calibrated probability for each option.

“This model is designed for routing, classification, prioritization, verification, and workflow control, making it easier to incorporate decision intelligence into existing applications, agents, and workflows in a secure, trusted environment,” Achint Srivastava, VP of Software Engineering in Microsoft’s Office of the CTO, explained.

How Microsoft-Decision-1 works

Microsoft said it evaluated the model across 36 benchmarks covering nearly 150,000 questions, with the benchmarks kept blind from training. In the company’s benchmarking, Microsoft-Decision-1 was 2.5 times faster than H2O-Lightning-4B v1.1, the runner-up on speed, and about 35 times faster than GPT-6 Sol in median latency.

Accuracy, latency and calibration, side by side (Source: Microsoft)

The probability scores indicate the model’s confidence in each answer and can help an application decide whether to act, defer a decision or request a review. Microsoft advises developers to validate the model and confidence thresholds on examples representative of their intended use.

Microsoft-Decision-1 was post-trained from Qwen3.5-9B for single-pass scoring. The company plans to base future versions on other models, including those from Microsoft AI and OpenAI.

The model supports yes/no questions, multiple-choice questions, rating scales and rubric-based grading of AI responses and agent actions through structured API calls. It is not designed for open-ended text generation, conversation, translation or summarization.

The company identified speed, performance across tasks, robustness, probability calibration and safety as challenges in developing the model.

govde:
Low-cost Android phones are arriving with malware that owners can’t uninstall

People who buy low-cost Android phones from online marketplaces may be carrying malware that was placed on the device before it reached them, Bitdefender has found.

The campaign, dubbed Midnight Mimosa, runs on budget Android devices from different brands built on MediaTek platforms. The malware ships in the device firmware, is present before the owner switches the phone on for the first time, and can’t be uninstalled.

“The compromise is complete before the phone is first switched on,” Bitdefender noted.

“The malware runs with system-level privileges that allow it to silently install and remove apps, grant permissions, and load arbitrary code supplied remotely. This essentially means its operators could install and delete apps at will, tuning each device to their needs, including making them part of large botnets.”

According to Bitdefender, the scheme is likely designed to generate revenue.

“The operators carry out ad and click fraud, collect device and installed-app information, and turn infected devices into residential-proxy relay nodes, making them zombies in botnets. This creates an additional revenue stream, as access to botnets for DDoS attacks is a hot commodity. The larger the botnet, the more money they can charge,” they added.

The campaign was observed on thousands of unique devices in more than 150 countries. Mexico, France and Italy lead the list, followed by the United States, Germany, Brazil and Spain.

A number of the affected models are counterfeits that borrow flagship names. Model strings include “i17 Pro Max”, “S25 Ultra”, “S24 Ultra” and “Note 18 Ultra”, and some devices that aren’t made by Samsung report the Galaxy S25 Ultra model code SM-S938B.

baslik: 2026-016: Critical Vulnerability in GitLab CE and EE
govde:
Release Date:12-10-2026 12:57:02

_History:_

*   _12/10/2026 --- v1.0 -- Initial publication_

## Summary

On 12 October 2026, GitLab released versions 19.4.2, 19.3.4 and 19.2.8 of GitLab Community Edition (CE) and Enterprise Edition (EE), fixing 24 security issues among which a **critical vulnerability** that could allow an **unauthenticated attacker** to **execute arbitrary code** on the server [1].

CERT-EU strongly recommends upgrading self-managed GitLab CE/EE instances to a fixed version as soon as possible, starting with internet-facing instances.

## Technical Details

The vulnerability **CVE-2026-97229**, with a CVSS score of 10.0, is located in the CI/CD regular expression compiler [1]. Weak validation of regular expressions leads to an **integer overflow**, and a specially crafted expression in a CI/CD configuration can then **trigger code execution** [1].

The same release also fixes other vulnerabilities [1]:

*   **CVE-2026-92883** (CVSS: 8.7): a **cross-site scripting** flaw in syntax highlighting that lets an **authenticated user run arbitrary JavaScript in other users' browsers** through a crafted repository [1].
*   **CVE-2026-16301** (CVSS: 8.5): an **authorisation flaw** that lets **a developer run pipelines on protected branches without permission** [1].
*   21 further issues, including a cache poisoning bug rated 8.2 that could expose protected CI/CD variables [1].

## Affected Products

The vulnerabilities affect the following versions of self-managed **GitLab CE/EE** instances [1]:

*   before 19.4.2
*   before 19.3.4
*   before 19.2.8

## Recommendations

CERT-EU strongly recommends upgrading all self-managed GitLab CE/EE instances to a fixed version, starting with internet-facing instances [1].

## References

[1] [https://docs.gitlab.com/releases/patches/patch-release-gitlab-19-4-2-released/](https://docs.gitlab.com/releases/patches/patch-release-gitlab-19-4-2-released/)

baslik: Four-Byte Write and Timing Bug Let Researchers Run Code in Windows SmartScreen Enclave
govde:
Security researchers ran their own code inside a protected part of Windows that is meant to stay sealed off even when the rest of the computer is taken over.

The protected area is a VBS enclave, an isolated slice of memory the operating system uses to guard secrets, and the one they broke into handles passwords for a Windows anti-phishing feature.

The work was done in a lab as a proof of concept, has not been seen in real attacks, and Microsoft fixed the flaw in its September 8, 2026 update.

The flaw is tracked as CVE-2026-83498. Microsoft rates it an elevation-of-privilege issue, Critical, with a CVSS score of 7.8, and says it has not been exploited and was not publicly known before the fix. Microsoft also says it found the same issue internally. The research, by the security firm Doyensec, was published October 13, more than a month after the patch.

A VBS enclave is a signed library that a normal Windows program loads but cannot read or change once it is running. The Windows hypervisor keeps the enclave's memory in a more trusted world, called VTL1 or Isolated User Mode, that ordinary code in the normal world, VTL0, cannot reach, according to Microsoft.

The design is meant to protect what is inside even if an attacker has already taken over the normal kernel or is running as SYSTEM. Running attacker-chosen code inside that world is what makes this research notable.

The enclave Doyensec attacked is SFAPE.dll, the component behind Enhanced Phishing Protection in Microsoft Defender SmartScreen. That feature watches text you type or paste and warns you if you enter your Windows sign-in password into an unsafe place, such as Notepad or a phishing page.

To do this without exposing the password, Windows intercepts it at login and stores it in hashed form within the enclave, so later inputs can be checked against it. On a Windows 11 system, the program that loads this enclave is lsass.exe, the process that handles sign-in credentials and runs as SYSTEM.

baslik: Microsoft Patches Record 1,413 Flaws, Including Exploited Windows Shell Bug
govde:
Microsoft on Tuesday shattered its own Patch Tuesday record by shipping patches for a whopping 1,413 vulnerabilities, including one that it said has come under active exploitation.

These include 1,102 flaws in Windows, 134 in Office, 61 in Developer Tools, 36 in SharePoint Server, and 22 in SQL Server. Of these, more than 670 relate to privilege escalation, followed by over 300 remote code execution flaws and 250 information disclosure flaws. Over 70 flaws are rated Critical in severity.

"Hundreds of CVEs in a single release used to be the exception; now it's the baseline," Dustin Childs, head of Threat Awareness at the Zero Day Initiative (ZDI), said. "Is AI to blame? Partly. It's accelerating bug-hunting on both sides of the fence, so vendors are finding (and fixing) more flaws, and researchers are finding them faster too."

"But AI isn't creating these bugs out of thin air; it's just shortening the time between a vulnerability existing and someone noticing it. The volume isn't the real story anymore. What matters is that discovery is scaling faster than exploitation, so teams that triage by sheer CVE count instead of exploitability are burning cycles on the wrong bugs. Patch what's proven, prioritized, and public, and treat everything else as this month's new normal."

The three vulnerabilities of note are listed below -

CVE-2026-96951 (CVSS score: 8.8) - A command injection vulnerability in Windows Shell that allows an unauthorized attacker to bypass a security feature over a network.

CVE-2026-108398 (CVSS score: 8.8) - An untrusted search path vulnerability in .NET Framework that allows an authorized attacker to bypass a security feature locally.

CVE-2026-92707 (CVSS score: 5.3) - An improperly controlled sequential memory allocation vulnerability in MessagePack-CSharp that allows an unauthorized attacker to deny service over a network.

govde:

The frontier AI lab said small AI models could form autonomous, self-propagating worm botnets that are "challenging to shut down," since "there's no centralized point to shut off."

"Such an 'AI worm' could carry its model weights with it as it reproduces (or re-download them from a public hub), and then run inference directly on compromised hardware," Anthropic said. "Effectively, the weights would become part of the malware payload."

The idea, at a high level, explains how AI models could potentially break into internet-connected devices and use their computing power to run themselves and spread to other devices, without having to rely on expensive data centers all the time. A more powerful model that's too large to fit into a single device could be split into small chunks and run across multiple machines to collectively run it.

baslik: Docker Fixes Critical Two-Year-Old Hub Flaw That Let One User Push Images as Another
govde:
A flaw in Docker Hub, the registry where container images are published and downloaded, let one user push, pull, or delete images as another user. Docker fixed the flaw on September 30 and says it found no evidence that anyone exploited it.

The flaw was in the feature that converts a personal account into an organization, Docker said in a security advisory on October 12. Conversion transferred the account's personal access tokens (PATs) to the user designated as the organization's owner. A PAT is used in place of a password in the registry, and the person who created each token can still use it.

The access was limited to the registry. It did not reach the Docker Hub web interface, and it could not be used to change a password, email address, or two-factor settings, or to take over an account.

Docker tracks the flaw as CVE-2026-105445 and rated it critical. The CVE record it published on October 13 gives the flaw a CVSS 4.0 score of 9.4.

The flaw was open from August 26, 2024, until the fix, a little over two years. Docker made the fix on Docker Hub itself, so there is no update to install.

Docker Hub cannot move a repository from one account to another. A user instead converts a personal account into an organization that keeps the same name, and must name an existing account as its owner.

Each personal access token acts as the account that owns it, at a permission level chosen when the token is created. While the flaw was open, conversion changed the owner recorded for each token and left its secret unchanged.

An attacker could abuse this by creating a token on an account they controlled, converting that account into an organization, and naming another user as its owner. The token would then work at the registry as that user.

The named owner was not asked to confirm the change and was not notified, according to Docker and the researchers who reported the flaw. Docker's conversion page has included the sentence "The new owner receives a notification email" si

Affected: Connect Secure "before version 25.1.3.0"

Not affected: version 22.7R2.14 "or prior"

Listed as unaffected: versions 22.8R2.5, 25.1.3.0 and 25.1.3.1

Ivanti tells customers to upgrade and to run its Integrity Checker Tool regularly. That tool misses this chain, Volexity said, because the exploit changes library code only in memory and restores the configuration data it alters. The attacker also took steps to stay hidden from the tool.

baslik: SAP Discloses Critical CVSS 10 Flaw in Cloud SDK for Python Allowing OAuth2 Credential Theft
govde:
A flaw in SAP's Cloud SDK for Python can send an application's OAuth2 client credentials to a server an attacker controls, SAP said in a security advisory on October 13. The flaw affects multi-tenant applications on SAP Business Technology Platform (BTP) that use the SDK, SAP's official Python client for BTP services. An attacker must be able to control the tenant subdomain, the name such an application passes to the SDK to say which tenant a request is for.

The flaw is tracked as CVE-2026-89111 and carries SAP's CVSS score of 10.0 out of 10. The advisory names version 0.45.2, released on August 21, as the fix.

The SDK handles authentication for those services with the application's client credentials, a client ID and a client secret. Version 0.45.2 added a check that rejects any tenant subdomain that is not a simple name.

Six later releases do not apply that check in every case, The Hacker News found. Versions 0.53.0 through 0.55.0, published between September 10 and September 18, skip it when an application calls the SDK's Destination service module.

Version 0.53.0 moved that module onto new shared code for requesting tokens, and that code did not include the check. Version 0.55.1 added it there on September 18.

Passing a tenant subdomain that contains URL delimiters "now raises ValueError immediately instead of silently routing credentials to an attacker-controlled endpoint," the 0.55.1 release notes say.

The Hacker News ran SAP's own tests for the check on October 13, against the source code of every release from 0.45.1 to 0.58.4 and of the three 0.36 releases. The six releases failed 9 of the 11 tests SAP added with version 0.55.1. That version and the 11 releases after it passed all 11.

As of October 13, the advisory lists no version above 0.45.2 as affected. Neither it nor the release notes say whether the six releases fall under CVE-2026-89111.

baslik: GitHub Tightens npm Publishing After Flaw Left 1,500+ Packages Vulnerable to Hijacking
govde:
GitHub has taken the step of expiring unvalidated npm trusted publishing configurations 48 hours after creation after researchers found that it was possible for an attacker to push new versions of a different user's package without having to steal their credentials.

"Your configuration becomes validated and exempt from expiry after its first successful publish," the Microsoft-owned subsidiary said. "Changing the repository or project identity requires a new trust relationship with a fresh 48-hour validation window -- ordinary edits don't restart the deadline."

The change contains the risk associated with trusting a repository or project name that changes ownership, GitHub said, adding npm also rejects trusted publishing tokens from GitHub Actions issue_comment events going forward, along with the Existing pull_request_target restriction.

In an update to its documentation, GitHub states that a newly created trusted publisher configuration must complete its first successful publish within two days, which validates the configuration and binds it to the "repository's immutable identity."

The development comes in response to findings from Bloom Security, which discovered a loophole within npm's trusted publishing to take over thousands of packages and trigger a Shai-Hulud-style cascading supply chain attack. The findings were reported to GitHub on June 6, 2026.

"Imagine this: an attacker compromises a single package. An AI agent on a popular package maintainer's device autonomously pulls it for a project," security researcher Golan Myers said. "That single endpoint is used to push malicious code to the popular package. All the package users are exposed. All because one person with the correct access was exposed."

Trusted publishing was introduced in npm in July 2025 as a credential-free authentication method that allows developers to push npm packages from a CI/CD platform, such as GitHub Actions, using OpenID Connect (OIDC) tokens.

baslik: LG Smart TVs Vulnerable to Pre-Auth Root Takeover From Local Network
govde:
Three vulnerabilities in LG's webOS can be chained to give an attacker on the same local network root access to certain smart TVs without a PIN or any interaction from the owner.

LG has issued a fix, according to an advisory published by SSD Secure Disclosure on October 12.

The chain was tested on two TV models, the 32LQ636BPSA and the 27TQ600SW, running webOS 7.5.7-25 on firmware 04.54.40. Whether other models or firmware versions are affected is not known.

Owners of affected TVs should check for a firmware update. No workaround is available for those who cannot update yet.

The attack enters through a service that the TV exposes on port 3001, which is used by the LG ThinQ app for pairing. An attacker replays a manifest from sync-demo, a built-in app already on the device, signed with a test certificate the firmware trusts. A permission in the manifest causes the pairing service to skip the PIN prompt and hand over a privileged key.

With that key, the attacker launches another built-in app, cmp-client, and points it to an attacker-controlled page. The app does not check where it navigates, and the loaded page keeps access to PalmServiceBridge, an internal interface to the TV's system services.

Through that bridge, the attacker calls the system logging service, pmlogd, passing shell commands through an input field the service does not check. Because pmlogd runs as root, the injected command runs as root.

This is not the first time the local network attack surface has led to root access on LG smart TVs. In 2024, Bitdefender disclosed a different set of webOS vulnerabilities that also allowed unauthenticated access from the network, affected different components, and were patched in March 2024. A separate chain demonstrated at TyphoonPWN 2025 used a path traversal on a different port.

The chain was demonstrated by an anonymous researcher who won third place in the LG webOS category at TyphoonPWN 2026, held in Seoul in May. No CVE identifiers have been assigned,

baslik: Attackers Heat French Supermarket Fridges Up to 50°C by Hijacking Danfoss Controllers
govde:
Attackers took remote control of fridges and freezers at hundreds of French supermarkets on the night of October 11 and warmed them, forcing stores to throw food away, several retail chains said.

The attackers reached them through the controller that runs all of a store's fridges and freezers, a device made by Danish company Danfoss that maintenance firms can manage remotely. Les Mousquetaires, which owns the Intermarché chain, said its fridges and freezers were put into defrost and heated to as much as 50°C.

CERT-FR, the French government's computer emergency response team, said in an alert published in French on October 12 that it is aware of numerous compromises affecting two Danfoss controller series, the AK-SM and the AK-SC. It told operators to disconnect the controllers or filter access to them.

CERT-FR is part of ANSSI, France's national cybersecurity agency. ANSSI's head, Vincent Strubel, called it urgent to take the two series off the internet or filter access very tightly, AFP reported.

Neither French authorities nor Danfoss has so far said who carried out the attack or how the attackers got into the controllers. Danfoss said most of the units hit were older models that it no longer updates.

Which Chains Were Hit

The chains gave their own figures to AFP, Reuters and broadcaster RTL. Each counts the stores the attack reached.

baslik: Ghostscript flaw lets hackers hijack servers via PDF uploads
govde:
A critical heap buffer overflow vulnerability (CVE-2026-39919) in the Ghostscript interpreter and rendering engine could allow remote code execution through specially crafted PDF files.

The flaw was discovered on August 23 by researchers at Defiant's platform Wordfence using their Argus AI-powered system.

Ghostscript is a PostScript and PDF interpreter that can render PDFs as images, generate thumbnails for previews, and optimize PDF files by compressing embedded images and removing unnecessary font data.

When generating a PDF thumbnail, WordPress can use the PHP Imagick extension to call ImageMagick, which launches Ghostscript.

A specially crafted PDF file containing a JPEG 2000 image can trigger incorrect handling of low-bit-depth samples and mismatched component resolutions.

Using Argus, the researchers developed two exploits for CVE-2026-39919 that force Ghostscript to write 1,024 bytes into a 256-byte buffer, corrupting nearby memory and leading to unauthenticated remote code execution in a WordPress deployment.

Wordfence focused on WordPress systems, but notes that the flaw affects any online system running Ghostscript 9.21 through 10.07.1 and is exploitable if the payload is adjusted to the environment.

The researchers tested ten Linux environments, including Debian, Ubuntu, Fedora, Alpine, and AlmaLinux, as well as an official WordPress Docker image snapshot, and found that all contained the vulnerable code.

The researchers tested two proof-of-concept (PoC) exploits and found that their ability to trigger the vulnerability depended on the target environment.

In a lab testbed, they executed the exploits 10,240 times against Linux packages but failed to achieve remote code execution. However, they successfully executed code remotely on a purpose-built test server.

The researchers found that modifying the PDF's fonts, language settings, font configuration, and one core system library enabled the exploit to succeed, although not reliably.

govde:
Anthropic is warning that small AI models could soon be able to self-replicate across consumer IoT devices, from Android TV boxes to smart ovens, creating distributed botnets capable of running AI workloads without relying on data centers.

“Our experiments suggest that small AI models may be months away from being capable enough to self-replicate on commercial internet-of-things (IoT) devices, like smart ovens and off-brand Android TV boxes,” Anthropic warns.

“ A replicator like this would be challenging to shut down, since there’s no centralized point to shut off—though it may be slow (with a doubling time of days).”

Replication experiment

The experiment used a simplified setting where the targets exposed unauthenticated ADB access.

baslik: Docker Hub flaw let attackers impersonate users, tamper with images
govde:
Docker has disclosed a critical vulnerability (CVE-2026-105445) in Docker Hub that let attackers access another user’s container repositories using a personal access token (PAT).

Docker Hub is an online registry for storing, sharing, and downloading container images - templates that package everything needed for an application to run in an isolated environment.

In Docker Hub, a PAT serves as a secret used to authenticate tools and workflows. It allows you to pull, push, or delete container images.

According to a security bulletin from the Docker team, an attacker could create an account and PAT, then convert the account into an organization and name a target user as its owner.

The CVE-2026-105445 flaw stems from Docker Hub reassigning a personal access token (PAT) to a designated organization owner without changing its secret or obtaining the target's consent. This allowed the attacker to use the token to authenticate as the target.

Depending on the token’s scope and the target’s permissions, attackers could pull, push, or delete images in the target’s repositories and accessible organizations.

“Within the scope of the token, a re-assigned PAT acted as the target user at the registry level, meaning an attacker could potentially pull, push, and/or delete images in the target’s repositories and in organizations where the target had access,” Docker explained.

“Because that includes publishing images under a legitimate name, we treated this as a software supply chain risk and rated it critical.”

Although the flaw is critical, Docker noted that it did not provide Docker Hub web access or allow attackers to change passwords, email addresses, or two-factor settings, potentially locking legitimate account holders out.

The vulnerability was introduced on August 26, 2024, when the conversion started reassigning the personal account PAT to the new owner. This occurred without revoking or rotating the secret, and without asking the named owner to confirm the change.

baslik: The MFA Gaps Attackers are Still Exploiting
govde:
On August 4, 2026, an Akira ransomware affiliate began spraying passwords against a SonicWall SSL VPN. Around seven minutes later, one attempt succeeded. The credentials were valid, and the VPN account had no multi-factor authentication (MFA) protecting it. Roughly two hours later, the attacker used RDP to access the domain controller and began enumerating Active Directory.

The ransomware deployment ultimately failed, but by then the attacker had already stolen credentials and file-share data.

It highlights an issue that is still common in 2026, where an organization might require MFA for Microsoft 365 and other SaaS applications while leaving certain access paths protected only by passwords. It’s this gap that attackers are regularly exploiting.

Stolen Credentials Remain a Valuable Tool for Attackers

Once an attacker has a valid account, they can begin interacting with the environment through the same authentication mechanisms used by legitimate employees and administrators. AI is adding another dimension to this problem by helping attackers operate at greater speed and scale.

The underlying identity tactics are largely unchanged: attackers still compromise identities, reuse credentials, escalate privileges and misuse legitimate access. The threat is that AI makes familiar techniques cheaper and easier to run at scale.

Mandiant’s ransomware investigations illustrate why that matters once credentials are obtained. Compromised legitimate credentials accounted for initial access in 21% of the 2025 incidents where the entry point could be established, typically through RDP or VPN.

RDP also appeared frequently later in the attack chain, with attackers using compromised or newly created accounts over RDP for lateral movement in around 85% of the ransomware incidents it investigated.

govde:
Microsoft today issued updates to fix more than 1,400 security vulnerabilities in its Windows operating systems and other software. Today’s epic patch batch dwarfs September’s record of nearly 1,000 fixes, which was already about ten times the normal monthly patch load from Redmond.

Just one of the weaknesses patched this week is considered a “zero day,” or already exploited in the wild. CVE-2026-96951 is a security feature bypass in the Windows Shell that affects Windows 10 and 11 systems, as well as some Server versions.

Windows 10 users might be wondering if they can still expect security updates after this month. Microsoft had been slated to stop shipping updates for Windows 10 systems in October 2025, but ended up adding another year of free updates after considerable pushback. A few months ago, Microsoft quietly extended that support for another year (until October 2027).

At least 78 of the flaws fixed this month are rated “critical,” meaning they could be exploited with little or no action by the user, and most of those critical bugs allow an attacker to execute code of their choice on the vulnerable system.

While Microsoft said there are no signs anyone is exploiting it yet, a security feature bypass in the .NET Framework (CVE-2026-108398) was publicly disclosed prior to today, potentially giving attackers advance time to work out how to exploit the bug.

Satnam Narang at Tenable said the number of flaws fixed this month far surpasses the previous record-setting year 2020, when Microsoft patched 1,261 CVEs.

“We’ve now crossed the 4,000 CVE mark with two months left to go,” he said.

Microsoft credits large language models for the high volume of bug discovery, and presumably AI gets credit for many of the patches used to fix these flaw. govde:
Anthropic Shows How Small AI Models Could Replicate Across IoT Devices

Anthropic researchers show how small AI models could autonomously replicate across IoT devices, raising concerns about adaptive, AI-powered botnets.

Anthropic published a paper this week that should make anyone who manages IoT infrastructure sit down for a moment. The research shows that small AI models are approaching the capability to replicate themselves autonomously across networks of cheap, poorly secured devices, the kind of Android TV boxes that sell for fifty dollars on Amazon.

The team ran a 26 billion parameter model, Gemma4-26B-A4B, distributed across 15 off-brand Android TV boxes networked together. It worked. The boxes collectively ran inference at 0.39 tokens per second, slow by any normal standard, but functional, and that’s the point.

The researchers broke autonomous replication into four steps: finding devices on a network, gaining access, setting up the AI model on a new device, and repeating the process. Previous studies had already shown that small models can handle many of the hacking tasks involved. This paper looks at a different question: can a model work out how to run itself on unfamiliar hardware? That’s a key ability for an AI worm that can spread across different devices.

A model with 9 billion parameters successfully set up inference on 8 of the 9 hardware types tested. Models with 30 billion parameters or fewer can already handle many of the individual steps needed for replication, although they still struggle to complete the entire process without errors. In the tests, only one model, GLM-5.2, reliably completed the full process from scratch. It spread to all 8 nodes in 4 out of 5 trials.

The researchers plotted the capability trend of small open-weight models against their release dates and drew a line.

govde:
Orphaned VBA Projects Inside DWG Files

Years ago I wrote diary entries about VBA code stored inside AutoCAD drawing files (.dwg).

In a nutshell: the VBA code is stored inside an OLE file, that is embedded inside the DWG file. You can do a brute-force search for the embedded OLE file, or you can follow a pointer inside the header of the DWG file.

I wrote a small Python script (autocad.py) for this second case. It looks at a 32-bit pointer at position 0x24 inside the DWG file. This points to a 16-byte long header, followed by the embedded file. This 16-byte long header contains the length of the embedded file. You use the script together with my tool cut-bytes.py, like this:

cut-bytes.py -S autocad.py -P AutoCAD : 461ed52aeb75384133a8238b2eb481ae5d505d4961effa622673d65a889c8218.vir.zip | oledump.py

This command carves the DWG file (inside the ZIP file) and extracts the embedded OLE file, and pipes it into oledump.py for analysis.

When the pointer is zero, there is no embedded OLE file, and cut-bytes.py returns nothing.

Recently, I discovered 2 DWG files that are an exception: their pointer to the embedded OLE file is zero, but if you do a brute-force search, you will find an embedded OLE file with a VBA project.

For example this DWG file.

Its pointer to the embedded VBA project is zero:

But it contains an embedded OLE file:

And right in front of the embedded OLE file, there is the 16-byte long header that contains the lenght of the embedded file.

Using the AutoCAD script to extract the file gives nothing:

But oledump.py can find the embedded OLE file and analyze it:

So while using oledump.py to analyze DWG files you find a VBA project embedded inside a DWG file, then also verify if it is not orphaned: verify that the pointer at 0x24 is not zero (or use the autocad.py script).

Microsoft today released patches for 1,417 vulnerabilities. 76 of these vulnerabilities are rated critical, with 7 critical vulnerabiilties requiring no customer actions. One vulnerability was disclosed before today's patch Tuesday, and one is already exploited.

baslik: Malware Indicators of Compromise (IoCs) | Recorded Future
govde:
Malware Indicators of Compromise (IoCs): A Complete Guide to Detection and Response

One malware hash can turn a vague alert into a concrete investigation. Analysts can search endpoints for the exact file, trace where it appeared, and determine whether related activity exists elsewhere. But if the attacker changes the file, the hash changes too. Domains and Internet Protocol (IP) addresses can also lose relevance as attackers rotate infrastructure.

This is why malware indicators of compromise work best as evidence within a larger investigation, not as isolated entries on a blocklist. Their value grows when analysts can establish where an indicator came from, how recently it was observed, what threats are connected to it, and whether those connections matter to their organization.

Malware indicators of compromise are technical artifacts or observations that suggest malicious activity. They help security teams detect, investigate, and contain threats, but an IoC is most useful when analysts can assess its source, timing, confidence, and relationship to other threat activity.

Malware indicators can include file-based artifacts, network infrastructure, and other technical evidence associated with malicious activity.

IoCs do not exclusively describe past attacks. They can point to malicious activity that may be underway or has already occurred.

Indicator types have different defensive lifespans. An IP address may quickly lose relevance, while a file hash remains an exact identifier for the same sample even if attackers create a new version.

Threat intelligence can add context that helps analysts prioritize IoCs, connect related activity, and move from an isolated match toward a wider investigation.

Ivanti customers are in familiar territory, responding to yet another actively exploited zero-day affecting one of the vendor’s most commonly targeted security products.

Volexity researchers, which discovered in-the-wild exploitation earlier this month, said attackers actually exploited three zero-days in a chain that allowed them to bypass authentication, execute code remotely and escalate privileges.

A threat actor, which Volexity tracks as UTA0576, exploited the defects before Ivanti addressed them and issued a patch.

“Because the issue was discovered internally, was not being actively exploited, and did not meet the threshold for an out-of-band release, a fix was scheduled for inclusion in our normal product release cycle,” an Ivanti spokesperson wrote in response to questions.

“Successful exploitation requires chaining multiple vulnerabilities and Ivanti has fully addressed the unauthenticated remote code execution component of that chain, eliminating the primary exploitation path,” the spokesperson added. “We are also developing additional updates to address the remaining vulnerability and further strengthen product security.”

The full scope of compromise remains under investigation. The company, in a security advisory, said a “limited number of customers” were already compromised prior to disclosure.

Federal authorities have charged 14 people and seized roughly 187 computers in their newest effort to disrupt North Korea’s remote IT worker scheme.

The Justice Department announced the indictment Tuesday, highlighting two arrests and searches of more than 40 residences in Texas known or suspected to operate as “laptop farms,” where facilitators maintain employer-issued laptops so North Korean engineers can use them while abroad.

An indictment unsealed in the Northern District of Ohio charges two U.S. citizens, Michael James Bostelle of Pennsylvania and Juan Cecilio Pena Carrillo of Texas. It alleges the two Americans, along with 10 others located in China, held remote jobs at more than 70 companies from 2019 through 2025 using stolen or fabricated identities, and collected about $3 million in pay.

An Ohio resident, Trey Michael Nolte, is also named as a co-conspirator in the indictment, but is not charged. Two unnamed defendants were also charged.“This investigation is about far more than fraud,” Ryan Raybould, a U.S. attorney in the Northern District of Texas, said in a release. “It is about a hostile foreign regime infiltrating American companies through stolen identities and covert access points inside our own borders. Every laptop farm we dismantle shuts down a revenue stream that the North Korean government relies on to fund weapons programs that threaten global stability. Operation Lonestar Roundup sends a clear message: we will not allow enemies of the United States to exploit our businesses or compromise our national security.”

This particular scheme proliferated over the past decade as remote work became more common. There have been multiple indictments since 2024 that have looked to charge willing conspirators in the U.S., while also disrupting the ability for North Korean nationals to successfully earn a paycheck. Despite those actions, the scheme has persisted. The Federal Trade Commission is asking a court to force the owner of multiple digital security and privacy companies from further operations, saying the businesses are serially defrauding their customers out of millions of dollars.

Earlier this month, the FTC filed a federal lawsuit in Ohio against Dmitry Belkin and 12 of his businesses, alleging they engaged in unfair and deceptive trade practices under the Federal Trade Act and violated the Telemarketing Act’s prohibition against deceptive and abusive telemarketing acts since at least 2020.

They operated websites like BlackmailHelpline.com, DigitalForensics.com and other sites that would routinely be advertised on Google, YouTube, X and other sites when users are searching for help with sextortion attacks.

The FTC alleges that despite taking in at least $60 million from customers, Belkin and his companies routinely failed to deliver most of the listed services meant to protect customers from ongoing scams, generated fake transcripts to fool customers into believing a sextortion threat had dissipated and routinely denied requests for refunds.

“Defendants falsely portray themselves as digital forensics experts, claiming they can track and identify sextortionists, prevent the spread of explicit material, and coordinate with law enforcement to bring criminals to justice,” the FTC said in its complaint. “Defendants further mislead victims by asserting that law enforcement will not help stop the sextortion attack” and that contacting the police is “the last thing you want to do.”

Participants heralded it as the largest joint scam operation to date, and the first focused on West Africa.

baslik: AI agents aren’t ‘going rogue.’ Frontier labs are skipping security basics.
govde:
Cyber experts say AI labs’ containment and monitoring failures — not agents with minds of their own — are to blame for recent alarming hacking reports. CISOs should vet their AI vendors and tighten security basics as safeguards.

Since July, US frontier AI labs and other AI leaders have revealed a string of incidents in which their models accessed external computer systems without authorization, events popularly described as AI agents “going rogue.”

The most well-known and studied of these incidents is OpenAI’s hack into Hugging Face, which OpenAI initially characterized as “an unprecedented cyber incident, involving state-of-the-art cyber capabilities,” and later said was due to “misaligned behavior,” or behavior its creators did not intend.

Following news of the Hugging Face incident, Anthropic revealed that one of its models gained unauthorized access to the production infrastructure of three organizations; Meta said one of its AI models hacked another company ​during cybersecurity testing; and Google confessed that its Gemini model carried out three “undirected computer hacks.”

Although press reports and the model providers themselves use language such as rogue agents or misalignment, cybersecurity experts who spoke with CSO argue that language obscures a simple truth: These incidents were caused by inexcusable failures by the frontier labs to implement cybersecurity practices that have been well-known for decades.

Compounding the problem, according to a half dozen cybersecurity experts CSO interviewed at three industry conferences in September and in subsequent conversations, is that the frontier labs, particularly OpenAI and Anthropic, have rejected their advice on how to improve their cybersecurity risk management practices to avoid these kinds of surreptitious hacks, often lumping cybersecurity practices under “AI safety,” in which they believe they have superior expertise.

The increased prevalence, and severity, of these incidents has many calling for more stringent guardrails and controls for agentic AI. In his personal blog, for instance, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella said the industry must “step back and assess the trust architecture for this new era.”

When quantum vendor IonQ on Sunday announced a $1.2 billion all stock deal to take over cybersecurity vendor Elisity, it spoke of a near-term future where enterprise quantum cybersecurity needs will move beyond replacing to-be-outdated encryption.

The acquisition brings together IonQ’s post-quantum cryptography (PQC) and quantum key distribution (QKD) capabilities and Elisity’s enterprise Zero Trust technology platform, IonQ said in a news release. “On a combined basis, IonQ will benefit from an expanded cybersecurity platform that both uncovers and protects against present LLM and emerging quantum threats.”

The news release pointed to more than 100 global Elisity customers, and said IonQ expects to receive “expanded channels to bring its PQC, QKD and quantum computing offerings to market for both enterprise and government networks, opening up the more than $10 billion microsegmentation market.”

Analysts and consultants saw the move as having potential, but pointed to technical challenges of truly integrating the product lines.

“What IonQ gets today is access. Dividing the headline price by those deployments puts it at about $13 million each,” said Frank Dickson, principal analyst at Dickson Research. “That is a steep price for a Rolodex, if you will. Paying in its own stock makes the price easier for IonQ to swallow.”

Dickson said that Elisity, which was founded in 2019, has focused on zero trust microsegmentation.

“In plain terms, it limits each user, device, workload, and AI agent to only the network connections it needs. An attacker who gets in cannot roam freely,” Dickson said. “Its software enforces those rules over the network a customer already owns, without new hardware. That is a solid business aimed at attacks happening today. Little of it has anything to do with quantum.”

baslik: Over 1,500 npm packages exposed by Trusted Publishing validation flaw
govde:
A weakness in npm's trust model could let attackers publish updates to legitimate packages by claiming abandoned GitHub repository names, researchers found.

A flaw in npm’s Trusted Publishing mechanism could allow attackers to hijack legitimate software packages by reclaiming abandoned GitHub repository names, potentially exposing millions of package downloads to supply-chain attacks.

Researchers at Bloom Security identified more than 1500 potentially vulnerable npm packages, including security scanners, authentication tools, and cryptographic packages.

The vulnerability, dubbed SlugFest, came from npm’s reliance on human-readable GitHub repository names to verify trusted publishers rather than the repositories’ permanent numeric identifiers. This could allow an attacker to inherit a package’s publishing trust by claiming a repository name that its original owner had abandoned.

The issue is now fixed, Bloom Security researcher Golan Myers told CSO. “The npm team confirmed that a fix had been shipped on October 2, introducing a 48-hour expiry for unvalidated Trusted Publishing configurations,” he said.

Myers said Bloom has not observed active exploitation in the wild, but confirmed that the flaw was successfully used to publish a new version of an existing npm package under their own controlled testing conditions. The fix addresses the exposure associated with unvalidated configurations, although maintainers still need to review their existing trust relationships, Bloom wrote in a blog post shared with CSO ahead of its publication on Tuesday.

A reclaimed repository name enabled package publishing

npm’s Trusted Publishing allows package maintainers to publish releases through automated workflows using OpenID Connect (OIDC), avoiding long-lived publishing credentials. However, Bloom found that npm’s trust configuration relied on the GitHub repository’s owner/repository name instead of its immutable repository ID.

baslik: Patching and preventing issues: What are the lessons you can learn?
govde:
Patching and preventing issues: What are the lessons you can learn?

In this Help Net Security interview, Kunal Modasiya, Senior VP & GM at Qualys, talks about why patching is still hard to get right. He explains how business pressure, revenue-critical systems, and patches that break things keep fixes from going out. Modasiya argues that speed alone has limits and that teams should look at the whole remediation workflow.

He discusses how proactive teams judge risk, why the gap between exposure time and weaponization time matters more than MTTR, and when automated patching makes sense on production networks.

The first issue with patching is that it involves much more than one patch to one issue. An update may require several patches to fully remediate the issue, or it may rely on configuration changes to fully deal with the vulnerability. So “simply patching” can be harder than it sounds, especially at scale.

The second issue is why patches sometimes can’t be deployed at all. Most security teams have experienced this: they know the issue exists and they have the update ready to go, but the business won’t allow them to implement it. Why? Often, these applications are mission-critical and directly tied to revenue generation. Stopping that application means stopping revenue, and that is a hard decision to get support for.

IT teams are also familiar with situations where deploying patches caused unintended consequences or additional impact that was not visible before, leaving the system down for longer than expected. Critical updates need the support of executive leadership and the board, and getting that buy-in may require a stronger case than just a security issue on its own. You must look at the financial impact and make the argument in terms the business understands and can get behind.

baslik: Meshery: Open-source cloud-native manager for Kubernetes
govde:
Meshery: Open-source cloud-native manager for Kubernetes

Meshery is an open-source tool for designing, deploying and managing Kubernetes infrastructure, built by Layer5 and its community and hosted as a Cloud Native Computing Foundation project. Teams use it to lay out clusters and applications on a visual canvas, check the design, and push it to multiple clusters and clouds from one central console, without hand-editing YAML.

Kubernetes runs on configuration files, and one wrong field or mismatched API version can sink a deployment. Meshery can catch those errors before a change reaches a live cluster. It runs Kubernetes’ own dry-run, a simulated deployment that applies nothing, and reports invalid resources, missing fields and version conflicts. Teams can wire the same check into a CI/CD pipeline so a faulty change fails before it ships.

Meshery draws the connections for you

Meshery works out how the pieces of a design connect, such as a pod mounting a persistent volume, an ingress routing to a service, or a cluster role assigned to a service account. It shows those links on the canvas and uses them to apply configuration rules. The rules run on Open Policy Agent, and users do not have to write its Rego query language.

baslik: Most companies count AI agents as insiders, and CISOs worry about their own liability
govde:
Most companies count AI agents as insiders, and CISOs worry about their own liability

Software that works on an employee’s behalf is now turning up in incident reports. At 95% of the companies in a Trellix survey of 600 CISOs, an AI agent or other autonomous system was linked to an insider incident in the past 12 months.

The agent logs in, reaches sensitive systems, and acts for a person using that person’s permissions. Most respondents already count it that way: 78% include AI agents and machine identities in their definition of insider risk. They work at companies with more than 1,000 employees in the Americas, Europe, the Middle East, and Asia-Pacific.

What barriers would your organization face when adopting AI or automation to manage insider risk? (Source: Trellix)

Most of the damage is still human

Among the 587 companies that reported an insider incident, accidental or careless actions by employees and trusted users made up 43% of incidents on average. Deliberate abuse by those same people made up 29%, and AI or autonomous systems 28%. The 95% counts any linked incident, so it says nothing about how many were serious.

The serious ones do exist. In June, an AI agent researching public medicine spending got unauthorized access to an Australian Government Medicare statistics portal, including non-public files. No personal medical information is believed to have been accessed. In July, AI agents broke out of a controlled test with reduced safeguards and compromised Hugging Face’s production infrastructure.

Fifteen hours is a long time

Respondents say it takes about seven hours to detect an insider incident and another eight to respond.

Part of the delay is sight. Sixty-three percent say they lack sufficient visibility into how employees use AI tools, and 68% say their policies do not address AI risks very well. govde:
Google quadruples Chrome bug bounty base pay, offers up to $20,000 for sandbox escapes

Google is updating its Chrome Vulnerability Rewards Program (Chrome VRP), increasing payments for memory corruption vulnerabilities and expanding rewards for other security flaws, fixes and research tools.

“A primary goal of the Chrome VRP has always been to identify ways to improve our internal testing by understanding which vulnerabilities are the most severe and challenging to uncover,” the company said.

Higher payments for memory corruption bugs

The base reward for memory corruption vulnerabilities is increasing fourfold to $2,000. These flaws can cause software to access or modify memory incorrectly, crash the browser or allow attackers to run malicious code.

In Chrome’s browser, network and GPU processes, rewards range from up to $4,000 for reads and crashes to up to $20,000 for controlled memory writes demonstrated from web content. Writes, use-after-free vulnerabilities and controlled reads can earn up to $10,000.

In the renderer process, which processes web pages, writes and use-after-free vulnerabilities can earn up to $8,000. Use-after-free flaws occur when software accesses memory that has already been released. V8 sandbox issues will receive a flat rate of $5,000, while V8 logic bugs will earn $4,000.

Rewards for medium-severity fixes and sandbox escapes

Google is offering a flat $2,000 reward for non-memory-safety issues assessed as medium severity, provided the report includes or directly leads to an identified fix.

The company is introducing rewards of up to $20,000 for high-impact, non-memory-safety sandbox escapes. These vulnerabilities bypass the security barrier designed to contain browser components.

Fuzzer bonus and year-end recognition

Google is reinstating a $2,000 Chrome Fuzzer Bonus for researchers who develop and contribute novel fuzzers, which test software with unusual or unexpected inputs to uncover vulnerabilities.

The Department of Justice disrupted multiple laptop farms across Texas allegedly being used by North Korean nationals to facilitate an IT worker scheme that allows the country to earn millions from U.S. companies.

The laptop farm raids, which were conducted September 21-25, targeted more than 40 residences, the DOJ said.

Law enforcement seized 187 laptops and other devices used by North Koreans. Such schemes have earned millions over the last eight years by tricking U.S. companies into hiring workers remotely into lucrative IT roles through stolen or purchased identities.

Alongside the raids, the DOJ indicted and arrested U.S. nationals Michael James Bostelle of Pennsylvania and Juan Cecilio Pena Carrillo of Texas. Several Chinese and North Korean nationals also were indicted. The department did not respond to requests for comment about whether the indictments and arrests were linked to the Texas laptop farm raids.

The DOJ indicted Bostelle and Pena on wire fraud, money laundering, and identity theft charges, accusing them of being key U.S.-based cogs in the IT worker scheme.

Bostelle and Pena helped a group of North Koreans earn more than $3 million from about 70 U.S. companies across 17 states, prosecutors said, including organizations in healthcare, cybersecurity, retail and manufacturing.

Large parts of the indictment are centered around U.S. national Trey Michael Nolte, who was not charged.

The DOJ did not explain why he was not charged, but prosecutors said he ran a shell company that facilitated the scheme. Nolte allegedly communicated with Chinese and North Korean nationals, recruited Bostelle, sent packages to China, received work laptops from U.S. companies and laundered the paychecks earned by the IT workers back to North Korea.

Sandbox vulnerability gives rogue AI agents a path to escape and leak data, research says

Cybersecurity researchers on Monday said they discovered a vulnerability in a widely used AI development sandbox that could allow rogue agents to leak sensitive information by bypassing restrictions designed to keep them isolated.

The new research, published by AI security startup AIR, found that a network filtering flaw in Vercel Sandbox — a tool used to run code in isolated environments — could allow agents to exploit certificate validation processes to transmit data outside approved networks.

“This vulnerability shows that enterprises can have Hugging Face [style] mini incidents with their own agents,” Niv Hoffman, AIR co-founder and CTO, told Recorded Future News in an interview.

“The new contribution our research makes is [showing] that even in the standard hardened sandbox of today, there are still flaws that will make an agent going rogue manage to escape the sandbox and do things in the wild.”

Developers typically use sandboxes to prevent AI agents from accessing unauthorized systems or transmitting sensitive information. Network allowlists restrict communication to approved destinations, preventing agents from connecting to untrusted servers.

AIR researchers found that rogue agents could circumvent those restrictions by exploiting the way servers handle digital certificates. In a scenario demonstrated by the researchers, a specific certificate was designed that could be sent to an approved server and could then trigger a request to an attacker-controlled server, allowing the information to be transmitted without the sandbox ever directly communicating with the unauthorized destination.

“A crafted certificate is all it takes,” the report said. “The wall meant to keep your secrets in has a door, and the agent holds the key.”

North Korean hackers have been targeting Ukrainian experts in diplomacy, security and international policy amid Pyongyang’s growing military cooperation with Russia, according to a new report.

As part of the campaign, the hacking group Kimsuky used fake conference invitations, research collaboration requests and malicious documents designed to steal information, South Korean cybersecurity firm Genians said in a report published Monday.

North Korea has provided troops to fight in the war in Ukraine as well as other military support to Russia since 2024.

"Kimsuky’s attacks against Ukraine may be aimed at collecting information on the war, the extent of North Korean troop losses, developments in the questioning and handling of prisoners of war, and the details of consultations between South Korea and Ukraine,” researchers said, adding that most of the observed attacks were unsuccessful.

Genians said the transfer of two North Korean soldiers captured by Ukrainian forces to South Korea in September could also be of intelligence interest to Pyongyang, particularly what the prisoners might disclose about North Korean military operations and casualties.

In one attack in August, the hackers impersonated organizers of a cybersecurity conference in Seoul and invited a Ukrainian security expert to speak at the event.

The email included genuine details about the conference and offered to cover travel and accommodation expenses. It initially did not contain malicious links or attachments. Instead, the attackers encouraged the recipient to respond before sending additional materials.

In another case, the hackers posed as a European policy researcher seeking feedback on a report about military cooperation between Russia and North Korea. After the recipient responded, the attackers sent a link to a malicious archive disguised as research material, according to Genians.

The Noise Inside the Network: How an Unsophisticated Attack Exposed a Third-Party Risk

By:Antonio DiazRuben Castillo

Published:October 13, 2026

Categories:Anatomy of an AttackInsights

Tags:Credential-based attacksIncident responseReconnaissance

Credential-based attacks

When unusual activity was detected on a European bank’s central IT system, its internal security team quickly recognized that the incident warranted immediate response. They discovered unauthorized VPN-based access attempts that spanned several months. They then engaged Unit 42 to determine the full scope of the intrusion, identify any persistent footholds and secure the environment.

While the activity appeared to be a stealthy cyberespionage campaign, the actual intrusion was made possible by gaps in foundational security controls. Rather than relying on novel techniques, the threat actor succeeded through persistence, exploiting weaknesses that stronger identity protections and basic security hygiene could have prevented. The case highlights an important lesson: Sometimes the most damaging intrusions begin with the simplest oversights.

Internal Reconnaissance: A High-Volume, Noisy Campaign

The intrusion originated through a third-party-managed external gateway appliance that was not properly configured to enforce strict authentication. Using compromised credentials, the attacker began by authenticating to internal systems. Once inside, the threat actor launched a discovery campaign of the internal network.

The threat actor conducted multiple rounds of reconnaissance, performing extensive host and network scans across a wide range of protocols and interacting with thousands of systems. This broad, noisy approach was less a targeted strike than casting a net to uncover as many access points as possible.

Others claimed last-minute relocations to divert devices mid-shipment. ## October 2026 Attack Surface Analysis

Preview Pane-triggered exploitation dominates this release with 23 CVEs across Office applications including Excel, PowerPoint, and Visio. These flaws require minimal user interaction; a victim could simply view a malicious file in the Reading Pane or file explorer preview, eliminating the traditional click-to-compromise barrier that many enterprises rely on as a user training backstop. The attack surface is substantial; any user who receives a weaponized document via download can trigger code execution simply by selecting the file. This class of flaw has historically been attractive to phishing operators and initial access brokers because it converts document delivery into reliable code execution without requiring macro enablement or a user opening the file.

Unauthenticated network-reachable RCE vulnerabilities appear across 15 CVEs this month, spanning Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol (DHCP) Server, Microsoft Quick UDP Internet Connections (QUIC), PostScript Printer Driver, and PDF handling components. These flaws allow remote attackers to execute code without authentication, making them high-value targets for lateral movement and initial network compromise. baslik: BSI rät dringend zur Absicherung vernetzter Steuerungssysteme
govde:
BSI rät dringend zur Absicherung vernetzter Steuerungssysteme

Ort Bonn
Datum 13.10.2026

Das Bundesamt für Sicherheit in der Informationstechnik (BSI) empfiehlt ausdrücklich, aus dem Internet erreichbare Steuerungsanlagen nach dem Stand der Technik abzusichern. Das BSI hat dazu eine Cybersicherheitsempfehlung veröffentlicht, in der die wichtigsten technischen Maßnahmen anschaulich beschrieben sind. Es handelt sich dabei um leicht umsetzbare Maßnahmen, die das Risiko erfolgreicher Cyberangriffe erheblich reduzieren. Die Empfehlung richtet sich insbesondere an Betreiber kleiner industrieller oder vergleichbarer Anlagen, etwa zur Kühlung von Lebensmitteln, Erzeugung von Strom und anderen Anwendungszwecken.

BSI-Präsidentin Claudia Plattner: „Die Vorfälle in Frankreich zeigen deutlich, wie Cyberangriffe unseren Alltag beeinflussen und stören können. Dieser Angriff hätte jedes Land treffen können und kann auch jetzt jederzeit Nachahmer finden. Derartige Einfallstore laden regelrecht zu Sabotage ein. Wir fordern die Betreiber solcher Anlagen eindringlich auf, ihre Systeme sicher zu betreiben! Die Sicherheitsmaßnahmen liegen auf der Hand und sind unkompliziert umzusetzen.“

Zu den Maßnahmen zählt zuallererst, den direkten Zugriff aus dem Internet auf Steuerungssysteme zu unterbinden. Daneben sollten VPN-Systeme und multifaktorgeschützte Zugriffe umgesetzt werden. Eingesetzte Systeme sollten auf dem aktuellsten Stand gehalten und Sicherheitsupdates und Fehlerkorrekturen kurzfristig eingespielt werden. Daneben ist zu prüfen, ob entsprechende Geräte oder Anlagen exponiert sind und dafür konkrete Gegenmaßnahmen zu treffen. Diese Maßnahmen sollten zur Routine gemacht und damit das Sicherheitsniveau deutlich erhöht werden.

baslik: Healthcare Sees No Relief from Cyberattacks Disrupting Patient Care
govde:
Healthcare Sees No Relief from Cyberattacks Disrupting Patient Care

New Proofpoint-Ponemon Institute report finds nearly three in four U.S. healthcare organizations experienced disruption to patient care due to cyberattacks

SUNNYVALE, Calif.– October 13, 2026 – Proofpoint, Inc., a global leader in human and agent cybersecurity, and Ponemon Institute, a top IT security research organization, today released findings from their fifth annual Cyber Insecurity in Healthcare report, revealing that cyberattacks are increasing in frequency, cost, and operational impact across U.S. healthcare organizations.

97% of organizations surveyed experienced at least one cyberattack in the past 12 months, of which 74% reported disruption to patient care as a result. The average number of attacks climbed to 51, from 43 in 2025, and the average cost of the most expensive cyberattack rose nearly 8% to $4.2 million. AI adoption is also outpacing governance, with AI agents operating without guardrails emerging as a leading cause of data loss, cited by 24% of respondents.

“Cyber resilience has become essential to healthcare resilience,” said Ryan Kalember, chief strategy officer, Proofpoint. “When a cyberattack delays a procedure, extends a hospital stay, or forces patients to another facility, cyber risk becomes patient risk. AI is now adding another dimension as people and AI systems access the same sensitive data and clinical workflows. Healthcare organizations need security built around those interactions so they can adopt AI without compromising the trust patient care depends on.”

Operational disruption is becoming healthcare’s biggest cyber cost

baslik: HSCC publishes AI clinical resilience playbook to help healthcare organizations manage patient safety, cybersecurity risks
govde:
HSCC publishes AI clinical resilience playbook to help healthcare organizations manage patient safety, cybersecurity risks

The Health Sector Coordinating Council’s (HSCC) Cybersecurity Working Group published the Playbook for AI Clinical Resilience (PAICR), a framework designed to help health delivery organizations manage safety, security and operational risks as artificial intelligence becomes increasingly embedded in clinical operations. The playbook addresses AI use across inpatient, acute care and outpatient workflows, where systems can influence triage, diagnostic assessments, patient monitoring, documentation, scheduling and care coordination.

The 26-page playbook equips cross-functional healthcare teams, spanning clinicians, governance leaders, IT and technical experts, risk managers and compliance officers, to detect, analyze and respond to threats in AI-integrated clinical operations. Accounting for workflow context, decision criticality and automation levels, it guides them from detection through patient safety review and regulatory response to system remediation, protecting patient safety, data integrity, compliance and operational resilience.

Determining how many playbooks are needed to address AI threats to clinical workflow, and of what types, depends on several structural, clinical and technical factors.

The first factor is clinical criticality and patient safety impact. Workflows with high acuity and low tolerance for error, such as emergency triage, ICU monitoring and surgical decision support, warrant distinct, highly detailed playbooks because AI failures in these settings can cause immediate patient harm. Lower-acuity or administrative use cases, such as scheduling optimization, can be grouped under broader operational AI playbooks.

baslik: ECSO outlines six priorities for EU space cybersecurity policy, from secure-by-design systems to threat intelligence sharing
govde:
ECSO outlines six priorities for EU space cybersecurity policy, from secure-by-design systems to threat intelligence sharing

The European Cybersecurity Organisation (ECSO) has called for a dedicated European industrial policy for space cybersecurity, warning that regulatory measures alone will not deliver the capabilities needed to protect the continent’s increasingly critical space infrastructure. The agency proposed a long-term public-private partnership to coordinate investment, innovation, intelligence sharing, certification and incident response across Europe’s space sector.

In a publication titled ‘EU Cybersecurity Industrial Policy for Space,’ ECSO said Europe needs a coordinated strategy focused on trusted supply chains, sovereign technologies and skilled talent as satellites and interconnected ground systems become increasingly important to navigation, communications, finance and climate monitoring. The report identifies the long operational lives of satellites, limited opportunities to update systems after launch and growing reliance on commercial technologies as distinct cybersecurity challenges.

The publication identifies six priority areas, including security-by-design across the system lifecycle, post-quantum cryptography, stronger ground-segment defenses, continuous security testing, supply-chain assurance and improved threat intelligence sharing. It also calls for measures such as zero-trust architectures, stronger identity and access management, cryptographic protection of command and telemetry links, software bills of materials and mission-specific cybersecurity training. ECSO said coordinated investment in these areas would support cyber resilience, competitiveness, strategic autonomy, European leadership and credible deterrence and response.

baslik: DOE, INL launch weekly series on cyber-informed engineering to advance cybersecurity in energy infrastructure
govde:
DOE, INL launch weekly series on cyber-informed engineering to advance cybersecurity in energy infrastructure

The U.S. Department of Energy’s Office of Cybersecurity, Energy Security, and Emergency Response (CESER) and Idaho National Laboratory (INL) are launching the CIE Back-to-School Weekly series to help energy professionals and engineers understand and apply the 12 foundational principles of Cyber-Informed Engineering (CIE).

Announced Tuesday, the initiative will publish new content each week through a learning hub, examining one principle at a time and explaining how the principles build on one another. The program aims to advance the integration of cybersecurity into infrastructure engineering and design, complementing traditional reactive cyber measures with engineered controls that use engineering and physics to mitigate cyber risks and eliminate catastrophic consequences from cyber-enabled attacks.

Each weekly module will include an overview of the featured principle, a case study demonstrating its application and key questions engineers can use to begin applying the principle to their organizations’ energy systems.

The learning hub opens with Principle 1, Consequence-Focused Design. CESER and INL also support CIE adoption through an implementation guide that helps engineers navigate questions for applying the principles and a web-based CIE Analysis Tool for tracking responses. A new CIE Handbook, intended to provide a simplified starting point for adopting the approach and connect users with related resources and research, will be released as the series’ capstone.

The series offers an in-depth look at each of CIE’s 12 foundational principles. baslik: Intermarché cyberattack exposes refrigeration security risks as French supermarkets face operational disruption
govde:
Intermarché cyberattack exposes refrigeration security risks as French supermarkets face operational disruption

French supermarket chain Intermarché was among several retailers in France hit by a cyberattack that manipulated connected refrigeration systems, raising temperatures in refrigerators and freezers to as high as 50 degrees Celsius (122 degrees Fahrenheit) and causing fires and food spoilage. Les Mousquetaires, Intermarché’s parent group, said about 150 stores were affected, with refrigeration units heated for six hours overnight. Carrefour reported attacks affecting 80 supermarkets, while Monoprix said 5% of its approximately 490 French stores were impacted.

France’s National Cybersecurity Agency (ANSSI) has been instructed to investigate, as authorities assess the potential for wider exposure. The attack highlights the cyber-physical risks facing retail operational technology (OT), as compromised refrigeration controls can disrupt food preservation and supply-chain operations without necessarily affecting point-of-sale systems.

Back in August, Claroty’s Team82 published research uncovering vulnerabilities on the Danfoss AK-SM 800A, a centralized system manager used to coordinate refrigeration controllers in supermarkets, cold-storage facilities, warehouses, and other commercial environments. The platform gives operators a web-based interface to monitor circuits, set temperature thresholds, review alarms, and manage users, and technicians often use it for remote maintenance. Team82 found numerous management interfaces reachable from the public internet, with a Censys scan showing 2,765 exposed devices.

baslik: UK expands AI-powered cyber defense pilots, prepares incident response measures as autonomous AI risks grow
govde:
UK expands AI-powered cyber defense pilots, prepares incident response measures as autonomous AI risks grow

The U.K. government announced on Monday a package of measures to strengthen national defenses against growing risks from increasingly powerful artificial intelligence (AI) systems, including expanding use of advanced AI to identify and address cyber vulnerabilities, considering stronger legal protections for essential services, and preparing for serious incidents involving autonomous AI agents. The initiative builds on two pilot programs that have identified and helped fix more than 1,000 potential cyber vulnerabilities across government systems and detected potential cyber threats.

The government said the expanded program aims to reduce immediate risks to public services while supporting wider adoption of AI-based cyber defense across the public sector. These measures also include examining potential changes to the Cyber Security and Resilience Bill regime to better protect essential services, including hospitals and utilities, from emerging AI-related threats such as autonomous systems operating beyond human oversight.

The move builds on two pilots that have already helped identify and fix over a thousand potential cyber vulnerabilities across government systems, and detect potential cyber threats. Extending the programme will help protect the public services people rely on every day to reduce risk in the short term, and support longer-term adoption across the public sector.

baslik: Space sector faces satellite cybersecurity blind spots, calls for stronger threat intelligence and information sharing
govde:
Space sector faces satellite cybersecurity blind spots, calls for stronger threat intelligence and information sharing

A cyberdefense researcher at the Center for Security Studies (CSS) at ETH Zurich has identified gaps in satellite cybersecurity monitoring that could leave space systems vulnerable to malicious activity. Clémence Poirier highlighted this in a World Economic Forum (WEF) story, citing a study that identified 407 cyber operations targeting the space sector in 2025, affecting at least 183 space-related organizations and involving 139 distinct threat actors. Hacktivist groups accounted for most identified actors, while distributed denial-of-service attacks were the most frequently observed activity. Other incidents involved ransomware, data leaks and credential theft, with cyber operations showing a correlation with major geopolitical crises.

Poirier noted that absence of documented cyberattacks against satellites in orbit does not establish that space systems are secure, noting that all 407 identified operations affected terrestrial IT environments at space companies, ground stations and user modems. Most satellites lack dedicated onboard capabilities to detect malicious cyber activity, limiting the telemetry available to analysts and their ability to identify attacker behavior and develop satellite-specific indicators of compromise.
